Marrow Controversy
MAR-oh kun-TROV-er-see
noun phrase (event)
Named for The Marrow of Modern Divinity, a 1645 English work (by "E.F.," likely Edward Fisher) that became the storm-center of a doctrinal controversy in the Church of Scotland from 1718 to 1723.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Marrow Controversy (1718-1723) was a doctrinal dispute in the Church of Scotland over the free offer of the gospel, the relationship of law and grace, and the danger of legalism (neonomianism) — sparked by the republication of the 1645 English work The Marrow of Modern Divinity. The controversy began when Thomas Boston commended the long-forgotten Marrow to others, and a new Scottish edition (1718) circulated widely. The book taught the free, unconditional offer of Christ to all sinners as sinners, the distinction between the law as a covenant of works and the law as a rule of life, and the believer's freedom from the law's condemning and covenantal power while remaining bound to it as a rule of gratitude. The General Assembly of 1720 condemned the Marrow, charging it with antinomianism and with teaching universal atonement and a kind of cheap grace. Twelve ministers — the "Marrow Men," including Thomas Boston and the brothers Ebenezer and Ralph Erskine — formally protested, arguing that the Assembly had, in its zeal against antinomianism, fallen into the opposite error of legalism: making the gospel offer conditional on the sinner's prior repentance or qualification, rather than free to sinners as sinners. The Assembly rebuked the Marrow Men but did not depose them. The controversy crystallized the Reformed doctrine of the free offer of the gospel: Christ is offered freely and unconditionally to all who hear, the warrant to believe is the gospel command and promise (not the sinner's secret election or prior worthiness), and this free offer is held together with both definite atonement and the abiding rule of the moral law. The Marrow Controversy remains a touchstone in Reformed discussions of the free offer, law and gospel, and the avoidance of both legalism and antinomianism.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A doctrinal dispute in the Church of Scotland (1718-1723) over the free offer of the gospel and the law-grace relationship, sparked by The Marrow of Modern Divinity; the Marrow Men (Boston, the Erskines) defended the free, unconditional offer against the Assembly's legalism.

MARROW CONTROVERSY, noun phrase. Doctrinal dispute in the Church of Scotland, 1718-1723.

Sparked by the republication of The Marrow of Modern Divinity (1645; Scottish ed. 1718).

The book taught the free, unconditional offer of Christ to sinners as sinners, and the distinction of law as covenant vs law as rule of life.

The General Assembly (1720) condemned the Marrow as antinomian; the "Marrow Men" (Boston, Ebenezer and Ralph Erskine, and nine others) protested.

Crystallized the Reformed doctrine of the free offer: Christ offered freely to all who hear, held with definite atonement and the abiding moral law.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Marrow Controversy is corrupted when reduced to obscure Scottish church politics, when the free offer it defended is collapsed into either Arminian universalism or hyper-Calvinist denial, or when the law-grace balance it secured is lost to either legalism or antinomianism.

expand to see more

Obscure-politics dismissal. To modern eyes the Marrow Controversy can look like an arcane 18th-century Scottish church squabble. Its doctrinal stakes are perennial: how the gospel is offered to sinners (freely and unconditionally, or only after they qualify themselves), and how law and grace relate in the Christian life. Every generation faces the twin dangers the Marrow named — the legalism that hedges the offer with conditions, and the antinomianism that dismisses the law. The controversy is a permanent reference point precisely because its questions never go away.

Collapsing the free offer. The Marrow's free offer is easily misread in two opposite directions. Arminians hear "Christ offered freely to all" and conclude universal atonement and resistible grace; hyper-Calvinists hear "definite atonement" and conclude the offer cannot be universal. The Marrow Men held the precise Reformed position both miss: the atonement is definite (Christ died effectually for the elect), AND the offer is universal and unconditional (Christ is freely offered to all who hear, and all are warranted and commanded to believe). The warrant to believe is the gospel itself, not the sinner's knowledge of his election. This is the narrow Reformed road between the two errors.
